bc_penny_lane.blurb: Penny Lane is a granite crack-and-corner wall tucked into the Smoke Bluffs, a short walk from town in Squamish. It is mainly a trad crag with a handful of bolted lines, and most of the climbing sits between 5.10 and 5.11, with a few easier lines and some 5.12s and 5.13s up top. It holds the namesake Penny Lane (5.9, trad), plus Crime of the Century and Quarryman. The wall catches plenty of sun, which makes it a nice choice on a cool day, and many of the cracks dry quickly after rain, though the bottom of the namesake route can stay damp for a while. Some edges are polished, so stiff shoes help. Bring a single rack with a few doubles in the smaller cams.
bc_penny_lane.parking_note: Use the climbers' lot for the Smoke Bluffs, reached from the Squamish highway through town by the Logger's Lane light.
bc_penny_lane.approach: From the lot, follow the signed trail up to the wall; the base of the main route sits right by a bench.

bc_sully_s_hangout.blurb: Sully's Hangout is a bolted sport crag in the forest above North Vancouver, reached on foot from the Lynn Headwaters trailhead. Every line is a sport route, and the grades climb steadily as you move from the left end of the wall to the right: a few easy warm-ups, a solid band of 5.9 to 5.11, and a short run of 5.12s on the right. Wingman (5.11b, sport) and Serene (5.11c, sport) are two of the better-known lines. The walk in is long enough that it is worth packing a full day's food and water, plus a headlamp if you plan to stay late. Expect a quiet, wooded setting rather than a roadside crag.
bc_sully_s_hangout.parking_note: Drive to the Lynn Headwaters lot at the end of Lynn Valley Road in North Vancouver and leave the car there.
bc_sully_s_hangout.approach: Follow the Lynn Loop trail uphill from the lot, then peel off toward the crag; it is a steady forest walk.

bc_petrifying_wall.blurb: Petrifying Wall is a steep, dark, water-streaked granite cliff in Murrin Park, beside the highway south of Squamish. It is mostly bolted single-pitch sport climbing with a smaller number of trad lines, and it leans hard: sustained, technical face climbing on small holds, with most routes in the 5.11 to 5.13 range and a couple pushing into 5.14. Black Water (5.12a, sport) and Mata Hari (5.12d, sport) are two much-repeated lines. The streaked faces hold moisture well into early summer, so the wall is best in the drier months of mid to late summer. It is a good place to come with fingers already warmed up, not for a first day on rock.
bc_petrifying_wall.parking_note: Park in the Murrin Park lot beside Highway 99, about 2 km north of Britannia Beach and roughly 9 km before Squamish.
bc_petrifying_wall.approach: A short, shaded forest trail climbs from the lot to the base of the wall in about ten minutes.

bc_lake_of_the_woods_bouldering.blurb: Lake of the Woods is a big, loose field of house-sized boulders on a lakeshore just east of Hope. There are no maintained trails inside it, so you scramble from block to block, and it takes some time to learn where the good landings and clean lines are. Landings are often sloped and uneven, with moss on some of the slabs, so bring several pads and a spotter. The problems run from easy to hard, with many in the V0 to V2 range, a scattering of mid-grade lines, and a few tougher ones up to V8. Dry days in the warmer months are the best bet. It sees fewer people than the other Hope boulders.
bc_lake_of_the_woods_bouldering.parking_note: Drive east out of Hope on Highway 1 for a couple of minutes; a small lot sits at the lake on the left side of the road.
bc_lake_of_the_woods_bouldering.approach: From the lot, follow the faint path along the highway barriers, then step down into the top of the boulder field.

bc_great_white_2.blurb: Great White is a long, west-facing cliff band in Sunny Valley at Skaha Bluffs, above Skaha Lake near Penticton. It is a mostly bolted sport crag with a few trad lines, and it covers a wide spread: easy intro walls on the left, then a big block of 5.11 to 5.13 on steeper, streaked walls where the cruxes are powerful. Wings of Desire (5.11c, sport), Test of the Ironman (5.11b, sport) and Air Test (5.13a, sport) are well-known lines. Sun starts hitting the wall in the afternoon even in midsummer, so spring and fall are comfortable, and mornings stay cool. Some routes on the harder walls have enhanced pockets, so grades can feel stiff.
bc_great_white_2.parking_note: Skaha Bluffs has a climbers' lot at the end of Smythe Road, reached from Lakeside Road; use the upper lot.
bc_great_white_2.approach: The Inner Loop Trail is the most direct way in from the upper lot and leads to the wall in roughly half an hour.

bc_east_wall_trail.blurb: East Wall Trail is a stretch of the Harrison Bluffs, a small granite crag in the forest between Agassiz and Harrison Hot Springs. The rock is fine-grained and grippy, with plenty of little pockets and edges. Most of the climbing is traditional crack and slab, with a smaller group of bolted lines, and the grades cluster at 5.9 and 5.10. Fresh Outta Purples (5.9+, trad), Shark Tooth Flake (5.10a, trad) and White Rabbit (5.10d, sport) are among the popular lines. The wall faces away from the afternoon sun, so shade arrives early, and the low elevation keeps the area usable well beyond summer. Mosquitoes can be thick in spring, and the trail is slick when leaves are wet.
bc_east_wall_trail.parking_note: From Agassiz, drive toward Harrison Lake on Harrison Hot Springs Road; past the golf course a gravel track leaves the pavement, and the parking spot is by the power tower a few minutes along.
bc_east_wall_trail.approach: A marked forest path leads from the tower area along the base of the bluffs to this stretch of the wall.

bc_free_and_easy.blurb: Free and Easy is a granite crag in the Smoke Bluffs beside the Blind Channel, a short stroll from the parking lot. It is mostly trad with some bolted sport lines and top-rope anchors, and the range is unusually wide: slab and crack lines from the easy 5.4 and 5.5 grades up into the 5.12s, with plenty of 5.8 and a strong group at 5.10 to 5.11. Free and Easy (5.10b, trad) and Cragger (5.7, trad) are popular. The crag is somewhat more shaded than the cliffs above it, which helps on hot days, and the walk along the water is easy enough to bring beginners. Weekend crowds fill the lot early.
bc_free_and_easy.parking_note: Use the climbers' lot for the Smoke Bluffs, reached from the Squamish highway through town by the Logger's Lane light.
bc_free_and_easy.approach: From the lot, cross the small bridge, take the wooden boardwalk to the channel, and turn left along the water past Jug Slab, The Zip and Sidecar. It takes just a few minutes.

bc_split_asunder.blurb: Split Asunder is a small granite wall in the Smoke Bluffs that was lost to the forest for years and has since been scrubbed and re-equipped, so the lines are cleaner than the surrounding trees suggest. It is mostly trad with a few bolted routes, and the mix includes cracks, a chimney and crimpy faces. Most of the climbing sits at 5.8 or around 5.10, with a handful harder. Confluence Crack (5.8, trad), Arete Asunder (5.10b, sport) and The Flame (5.10a, trad) are good picks. Nearly every route ends at rappel chains, and the wall is set back up the hill from the main loop trail, so it tends to be quieter than the roadside crags.
bc_split_asunder.parking_note: Use the climbers' lot for the Smoke Bluffs, reached from the Squamish highway through town by the Logger's Lane light.
bc_split_asunder.approach: Take the loop trail to the foot of Lumberland, then climb a rough path up a short rise on the left. The wall comes into view among the trees at the top, a little way around a bench viewpoint.

bc_d_thighmaster.blurb: Thighmaster is a cluster of granite boulders in the forest at the foot of the Stawamus Chief, part of the Grand Wall Boulders. The problems cover the whole range, from easy V0s to a few hard lines in the V8 and V9 range, with a good middle band of V2 to V5. Sesame Street (V9, bouldering), Tim's Sloper Problem (V5, bouldering) and Treeson (V2, bouldering) are some of the better-known lines. The old-growth canopy keeps this corner shady and cool, so it is good on warm summer days and less pleasant when it is wet or cold. The walk from the parking lot is short, so it is easy to fit in after a multi-pitch day. Bring pads and a light jacket.
bc_d_thighmaster.parking_note: Leave the car in the Stawamus Chief lot by the campground, or the main Chief pullout, beside Highway 99 just south of Squamish.
bc_d_thighmaster.approach: From the lot, join the Apron Trail, then cut right into the trees; the boulders are a couple of minutes away.

bc_the_clean_boulders.blurb: The Clean Boulders sit along the Mamquam forest road under the north side of the Stawamus Chief. They are granite problems in the Squamish forest with mostly flat landings, which makes this a friendly area for a short session or a first outdoor day. A large share of the problems are V0, there is a good middle range, and a few hard lines reach into the V7 range. Hydrogen (V2, bouldering), Welcome (V4, bouldering) and Japanese Cowboy (V5, bouldering) are among the favorites. The first boulder is right across the road from the pullout, and the forest cover keeps things shaded and cool in summer. The pullout is small, so carpooling helps.
bc_the_clean_boulders.parking_note: From the Apron lot, drive 2.4 km up the Mamquam forest road to a small pullout on the left that holds only four or five cars.
bc_the_clean_boulders.approach: The first boulder is across the road from the pullout; the rest follow through the trees.
